text: We're at the offices of Dan Fulgham and we're going to be interviewing him about the Roswell incident.
We spoke about the investigation that was conducted last year.
The Secretary of the Air Force was asked by the General Accounting Office to look into some information about what's been known as the Roswell incident.
And we've looked into that and we wrote a quite lengthy report last summer and I provided you a copy.
And we've come to, after that investigation, we've come to determine that perhaps some of the people were relating not something that happened in 1947,
but something that happened to you personally in 1959. And we'd just like to ask what you remember about it.
Alright, this is Dan Fulcham and I will respond to your questions.
Okay.
If you could just start off with when you entered the Air Force and what some of the
positions you held throughout your career.
I came into the Air Force through the Aviation Cadet Program, graduating from flying training
at Bryan Air Force Base in March 22, 1952.
From there I went to gunnery training at Luke Air Force Base in F-80s and F-84s and proceeded
directly on to the Korean conflict.
As I recall, reporting in somewhere around August of 1952 to Fimcom Area B outside of
Tokyo for reassignment to the 474th Fighter Wing and F-84s at Kunsan, Korea. I flew 100
combat missions out of Kunsan and Daegu. The squadron that I was in was transferred sometime
time in the spring of 1953. As I recall, I finished my combat tour in approximately May
of 1953 and then returned to the U.S. and was assigned to Webb Air Force Base in Big
Spring, Texas as a flight instructor in T-33 and T-28 aircraft. That tour was a very special
I was in the crew training headquarters.
I was the command coordinator for aviation physiology, since I had gone through aviation
physiological training while at Webb.
Command coordinator for aviation physiology.
coordinator for what then became the Air Training Command. That sort of made me visible and
eligible for an assignment to the Aeromedical Laboratories at Wright-Patterson. I think
I reported in there in late 1957 to the Aeromed Lab and was placed in charge of all of the
high-altitude chambers at Wright-Patt. It was during that period of time I became
involved in the space program. The Air Force had a manned space program. There
was more all of the human activities of it were being run out of Wright-Patterson,
and the other year a med lab. And then when Sputnik went up and President Eisenhower created
NASA out of the old NACA and took all of that program work, transferred it to NASA, and
it became Mercury, became Project Mercury. And I worked in the Mercury program, still
still on the Air Force side. From Wright-Patt, it was off to Purdue for a master's degree
in human factors engineering in 1959. Graduated there in 1960 and reported to the Flight Test
Center as a bioastronautics project officer at Edwards Air Force Base. It was in the summer
of 1870. But Rife Patterson, though, that I became involved in the balloon training
program since I was an active instructor pilot in T-33s over at the flight test group. And
then Joe Kittinger had this program, had responsibility for several programs, as I recall, that involved
of palleted balloons, helium balloons.
And of course, it was more than one person could handle,
so Bill Kaufman and I were, had volunteered for
and been selected to train as balloon pilots.
It was during that period that we participated in the takeoff
and landing and flying time out of Holloman. In the call, both of the training flights
that we participated in before the accident occurred, all three of us flew on every flight,
those two. To get the verdict on that, to go back to the flight test center,
at Edwards. There in the bioastronautics group, in my background in parachuting, the commander
asked me to take on the additional duty of supervising the X-15 pararescue team, which
I did and that led me into more altitude parachuting in support of the X-20 and the Gemini program
in Central California. That all occurred in the mid-60s. In 1966 I was selected for an
assignment to Vietnam. I went through F-4 training at Georgia Air Force Base, reporting to the
fighter wing under Colonel Robin Olds in the fall of
1966, as I recall, it was about in October. I went flying combat almost immediately in the
attack fighter wing as a member of the Triple Nickel Squadron. 133 missions,
the north, some sixteen into my area,
group pack six, and finished up there in, I think it's, I recall in June of 1967.
To the U.S. in 67, I was assigned to Gunner Air Force Base in the Corona
Harvest Project, which was to write the history of the Vietnam War.
There I had an interesting assignment in 1968 to join up with the history office, Colonel
of Burton Shaw out of Pac-F in Hawaii and write the Pueblo incident from the Air Force
point of view, which was quite an interesting project. It took about weeks to do that. From
there I went back to Purdue for a Ph.D., reporting to Purdue in 1968 and graduating from Purdue.
assigned as chief of the flying training simulation group under the Human
Resources Laboratory at Williams Air Force Base. From 25 it was time I reported to
Brooks Air Force Base as vice commander of the Human Resources Laboratory and
then commander of the Human Resources Laboratory, the position from which I
I retired in August of 1978.
Commander of the?
Commander of the Human Resources Laboratory.
Rank was 06.
Since retirement from the Air Force in 1978,
I've worked in the civilian research business.
Still primarily in life sciences
and human factors research.
My present position is director of biosciences
and bioengineering for Southwest Research Institute in San Antonio. Eight years in that
position.
Okay. Well, now we'll go back to the situation that we think you may have been and become
a part of this mythology surrounding this Roswell incident. If you could just briefly
you became involved in this, the high altitude ballooning with Captain, now Colonel, Joe
Kittinger.
I don't remember the exact mode we took in order to get involved in the program,
other than we just, it was something different and we wanted to take a shot at it.
But essentially it was that Joe needed some support in several projects, one of which
was to fly a scientist to 80,000 feet in a balloon-suspended gondola to take pictures
of Mars from a gyro-stabilized platform.
Stargazer.
Stargazer.
And there were to be several flights in that project, and we wanted backup balloon pilots
for that.
Another one was high dive, as I recall it was called high dive, in which altitude jumps were to be made from an open gondola.
Since I was parachute qualified, I wanted to be one of the jumpers.
And Bill Kaufman was not jump qualified, but he volunteered to at least be one of the balloon pilots.
Yeah. There was some reason that he was involved, too, but...
First, it was mandated by the... it wasn't the FAA, that. It was probably the CAA...
that we had to have a license in order to fly in controlled airspace, if you will.
Nobody knew anything about balloon licensing.
This was before the hot air balloon would even have been invented.
Yeah, right. This was all helium, and the Air Force was the only military that could afford helium in those days.
So we did the majority of all the helium ballooning in the Air Force and Navy.
We went to the CAA, or whatever it was called in those days, and asked them to issue balloon licenses.
and the best they could come up with was a student pilot license.
And I think they just harbored trail.
They said, you've got to have X number of landings
and so many hours to be given your license.
Carl being the most qualified to instruct,
since he had quite a bit of balloon time,
we put together a program to go to Holloman
and accrue the number of hours of flying time and the number of landings necessary to qualify
Bill Kauffman and I as student balloon pilots, if you will, so we could participate in the program.
The first flight out was an all-night flight. In both cases, they were all-night flights.
In the first flight we terminated just north of Paso and recovered by helicopter and taken
back to the Holloman.
And the second flight was one in which we took off with the intention of landing at
Roswell at daylight, and that's exactly what the flight plan turned out to be.
landed just right in the outskirts of the city of Roswell just after sunrise.
Which was it, north of town or south? I don't remember.
I think it was north of town. Just the way I have that picture.
So we found it in the range record, it seemed to be that it was north of town.
Yeah, north of town.
So could you just describe on that second flight there, when you had the little miss out, and how that came about?
We'd been flying all night, and as daylight approached, and it became light enough to see the ground,
we valved off some gas and went down and started shooting practice landings,
touch-and-go landings, and Kittinger instructed us how to stand on the
outside of the gondola and when it touched down on the ground just jump off
and that would give enough rebound to the balloon that it would go bouncing
back into the air and that we didn't have to dump ballast right away. And you
You just had to scramble to hold onto the side of the gondola from the outside.
And Joe shot some landings to demonstrate,
and I shot a series of landings,
and then Bill Kaufman took over the controls,
the controls being a cup of lead shot in one hand
and the lanyard to valve gas in the other,
and you could adjust your rate of descent
and then time your touchdown so that you'd hit the ground with enough force to make contact
but rebound.
There'd be enough balloon inertia to come on down a little bit and then it would rebound
and take you back up into the air.
Give you the touching down.
A hundred feet or so, something like that.
It was now approaching sunrise, and of course what was going to happen as soon as the sun
cracked at rise and the wind would come up.
We knew that anything above ten knots of wind would probably wind up having to fly all day
and all night again before we could land, because it was just too dangerous to land.
and wind, of course, out in that desert, the wind came up and stayed up at 25, 30 knots all the time,
during the daytime. So we were approaching the town, we could see we were approaching the town,
and Joe or Bill said, I think it was Joe said, there's a clearing over there just this side of
of the highway where the school was located, and Joe said,
we'd better get down into that clarion because when it was coming up,
our lateral speed was increasing all the time.
He said, we'd better try and make that field,
or we may run out of any place to land.
We'll be downtown before we know it.
And so we valved gas at a pretty good rate to clear the trees
that surrounded that field and then to try and get a vertical descent rate
high enough that would get us into this open area. And how big it was, four, five, six acres maybe,
in size, maybe a few more than that, but not much more. Just prior to that, when we decided we'd
better make it a final landing, I said, why don't we clean up this cockpit a little bit, the gondola,
because our helmets were lying in the bottom of the gondola with some other crap down there. So,
So I picked up my helmet and put it on.
Everybody put their helmets on because we hadn't been flying.
Was the kid you were wearing that Canadian Hunter's hat?
I don't recall what Joe had on.
Bill had the same kind of hat I had on.
It was one of those bicycle helmets that was...
Yeah, Bill and I wore those.
Those were developed for SAC air crews.
You know, they had to go up and stay up 24 hours at a time, and a regular P-1 helmet
in those days was just so damn heavy and hot.
Well, I think that's what Kauffman has on.
He has the standard issue helmet.
Yeah, he might.
And then you have the experimental.
Yeah, mine was that SAC helmet that I had gotten.
It was as cool as I could.
The long missions they were flying.
Yeah.
But my helmet on, and it looked like we were going to be alright coming into the field,
even though our lateral speed was up a little bit.
And the way we effected our final landing was to, we had an electric squid,
and we could uncover the toggle switch, and when we activated the toggle switch,
which it blew an electric or sent electric charge to an explosive bolt that held the
balloon to the top of the parachute. And the technique was to let the gondola hit the ground
to kill some lateral speed and hit the switch before the balloon could rebound.
To cut loose the balloon?
Yeah, to cut loose the balloon. So before it rebounded, it carried the gondola back up again.
And what happened was Bill hit the switch just a fraction too soon.
And we still had too much lateral speed, but when the balloon cut loose,
The lateral speed was such that the gondola tin canned on the ground, which it just, like
you throw an open-ended tin can down on the ground and it just tumbled end over end.
I don't remember how many times it did that, maybe once or twice.
It seemed to rest upside down, and my position of the gondola was on the bottom of the stack,
with my head wedged in between the lip of the gondola and the ground. And Bill Coppin and
Joe Kittinger were on top of me so that I couldn't move because they were, their combined weight was
just pinned me to the ground. And of course they got that sorted out right, right quick and got
moved off the top of me and then we jacked up the gondola and turned it over on its side.
And we crawled out. I forgot the gondola weighed 600 pounds or something like that.
So we were trying to assess, you know, our state, the damage to the gondola. Nobody appeared to be
hurt. There was no pain or strain or anything, but Joe had a cut under his eye, and it looked
like it was about a half inch in length, but it was just bleeding like a stuck pig, and
it didn't look like a very deep cut either, where, you know, any facial cut bleeds quite
a bit anyway. But he appeared to be more wounded than he really was. It was not a serious cut
cut it off. I was moving around the gondola and doing the same thing the other two were,
just picking up equipment and seeing what the status was there. And I think the helicopter
came in about that time also.
Yeah. Sure. The H-21.
Yeah, but that's from the first flight.
Okay.
That is not the Roswell flight. That's the one where we recovered out in New
shorter brother would be pink.
But that's the same helicopter from Hollywood.
One tracked us all night.
That's the same one that came over and picked me up
and flew me back to Hollywood from the hospital.
During this moving around,
I reached up to do something about my face.
He had brushed up the guard,
didn't, no pain, no strain or anything.
and I felt my forehead out in front of the helmet.
I didn't realize it at first.
It just, there was something there like padding or whatever.
And so then when I pushed it over my fingers,
I realized it was my forehead.
And I thought, well, for Christ's sake, you know,
apparently damaged something because my forehead shouldn't be sticking out in front of the helmet.
So I said, uh-oh, I know I'm smart enough to know if I did something that I'm just not feeling yet
because there's no pain there or anything,
I may be injured to a point that I could go into shock or something and I keep moving around.
So I sat down immediately and took my helmet off.
helmet off my head started swelling not just my forehead but all of my head
started swelling and I found out subsequently from the doctor that what
had happened was I had crushed a lot of the blood vessels and the nerves
when that gondola had landed on top of my head and pinned me between it and the
the ground and did it on a, I recall almost a face-up attitude. So I got front and rear crushing
motion and it did crush those blood vessels and nerves and that's why I wasn't feeling anything
because the nerves were dead. And the blood, the free blood that was pouring out of these
capillaries and vessels were swelling my head. It had to go somewhere, and there was enough
free skin there that's loose enough to start swelling.
You felt it right away?
Yeah.
As well?
Oh, yeah, sure. When I still had my helmet on, I could feel my forehead puffed out in
front of my helmet. Now, that's not normal.
I wouldn't say that, no.
So, I still felt no pain, no problem, but it was getting to the point now that my face
was beginning to swell a little bit, almost liquid and everything, and finally my eyes
swelled shut.
My eyelids swelled shut, too.
Is this why you're still out there?
No, I think this was a progressive thing at the time I got to the hospital.
Okay.
The swelling was beginning pretty bad.
It ultimately got to the point where the only way I could see was to take my thumb and index
finger and spread my eyelids.
There was nothing wrong with my vision or anything other than my eyes were swollen shut.
I could spread my eyelids and see, and as soon as I let go, my eyelids snapped shut
again.
So now you're injured and you decided to lay down and figure out what's going on.
Well, I just didn't want to be up moving around in case my system was subject to going into shock.
I knew enough about physiology and after all we were in the life sciences business.
business. I knew that pretty well. I don't recall the exact sequence of events. There
was nothing spectacular, nothing notable or noteworthy about it. I wanted no matter how.
I couldn't see myself, so I didn't know how bad I looked. But I could tell by feeling
that my head was considerably enlarged, considerably enlarged. And it's the sort of thing where
But sure, I didn't feel bad. So when we arrived at the hospital...
So how did they get you to the hospital?
I don't... I thought we flew over in a helicopter.
I just, I remember, I think I remember getting out of the helicopter on the flight ramp at Roswell.
So it was probably a five minute flight, very short flight.
Very, very short. Very short.
Okay.
And also, as I recall, when we got there, there was not a doctor immediately available,
and I think they had to call the doctor to come to the hospital.
Do you remember anything about your arrival?
Well, if we landed on the flight ramp, we probably wound up riding an ambulance to the hospital, would be my guess.
Do you think you were walking, or did you lay down?
No, I was walking. There wasn't anything wrong with me. I felt fine.
In fact, I remember very clearly, even before either one of us were treated,
Joe Kepner and I sitting out on the front steps of the hospital smoking cigarettes.
Okay.
We went outside to smoke, and Joe's eye was still bleeding.
bleeding. Not profusely, but he was still bloody from that little cut on his face.
So you sat out there. Were there civilians in the area?
I don't remember seeing anybody until early in the morning.
And you don't believe...
What we were waiting for was a doctor to get there. And I recall at that time there was
this controversy going on with security in the hospital about who the hell were we anyway.
We weren't supposed to be there, and nobody knew anything about the Air Force officers
flying balloons, and we could have been intruders, you know, one of Curt LeMay's famous penetrative
security teams.
And I remember Joe trying to get ahold of Colonel Stamp to establish our identities
and who we were.
And I guess that occurred sometime during the morning.
In the meantime, the doctor showed up and he examined me.
He knew he wanted to do an examination.
You know, we better wrap that head in something.
So he used an ace bandage and wrapped my head to keep it from continuing to swell.
And I believe, I remember him discussing with me at that time as to whether or not we ought
to aspirate some of that fluid.
Decision, yes or no.
And I do know the decision was made, well, the helicopter was there, they wanted to fly
us back to Holloman.

So, I went back to the flight line in the helicopter, and at that time, as I recall earlier, you know, I couldn't remember whether I spent the night at Roswell or went back to Holloman, but the record seems to indicate that I flew back to Roswell, I mean to Holloman, when it is 21.
When your medical record shows you spending the night at a Harlem hospital.
And there was some kind of party that night, and I put on my uniform and went to the party.
And my head was wrapped in ace bandage, and my eyes were swollen shut.
I had to be led around, and I just took the position of help.
I felt fine. I didn't have a headache. I didn't feel bad.
So I just stood around in the crowd with my hand out, and there was somebody who always kept feeding me drinks and talking about how bad I looked.
My eyes were now totally swollen shut, black underneath, and I really didn't look swift at all.
Were people shocked to see you? I mean, did you look like yourself?
No, you couldn't recognize me. You couldn't recognize me at all.
was much bigger than it normally was.
Yeah, much bigger.
And this was that night.
The next day, or the day after, I guess it was the next day on Sunday,
the flight surgeon at Holloman says, you know,
he said, we've got to do something about that swollen head
because what will happen is scar tissue will form under there
and you'll be permanently disfigured.
He said, you probably already are going to be permanently disfigured to some degree.
So some of that swelling may never go away because of scar tissue and everything.
He said, what we need to do is aspirate some of that fluid out there
and compress it down and see what we can do.
According to your record, Dr. Leslie Leeson, and I spoke with him,
he aspirated 20 cc's of blood.
Yeah, so he came at me with one of those god-huge needles.
I forgot what size it was now, but...
Yeah, according to your record, he did, he aspirated the blood the day of the accident back in Holland.
Eight millimeters, something like that.
Twenty cc's of bloody fluid.
I didn't see what size needle he used. It was about an eight millimeter, is what I recall.
I just remember it was a big damn needle.
It didn't particularly hurt because my head was still numb.
You know, the scalp and everything was numb, but he did take a lot of fluid out.
rewrapped it again in a spandage to keep it down as tight as he could.
So in this picture... In that picture my head is considerably reduced,
considerably reduced from what it was. So this is back at Wright-Patterson
some days later. Yeah, this is back at Wright-Patterson. That's on Monday or Tuesday. Right, we had you returning on Sunday according to the record.
Yeah. It was, it had to have been on Monday or, well, that could have been Sunday afternoon.
You'd write that?
Yeah, I'd write that. I don't remember. I remember being in the airplane on the way back.
Okay.
But there was nothing notable about the flight that fixed it in my mind or anything like that.
We were just going back to Wright-Patt.
Okay. Before we move on a little bit, I just want to ask you what you remember about being at the hospital there.
You said you remembered arriving, smoking a cigarette at Walker Air Force Base.
And you remember having a cigarette on the front steps.
And you don't remember civilians being in the area.
I don't. I really don't.
Do you remember any nurses being in the area or assisting in the treatment?
I know. The doctor being there to, you know, talk to me about, does it hurt, and that's
sort of, you know, the typical medical exam.
Was there, how many doctors? Was it one, many doctors, or one doctor?
Just one that I remember. I don't remember seeing. There could have been other doctors
in the hospital, but only...
Who was he? Was he, to your knowledge?
I don't even remember if he was one of the flight surgeons or not.
He was one of the Air Force doctors assigned to the hospital.
Keep in mind, by this time, my eyes are swollen shut.
So I'm not seeing much of anything.
If somebody asked me a question or something,
and I thought I needed to see them to respond to it,
I'd pry my eyelids apart and look at them.
But other than that, when I talk to people,
So did they keep you like in an examining room or did you sit in a waiting room?
No, I didn't sit in the waiting room, but I was perfectly ambulatory.
I could get up and move around. I would or not, I might go into shock also.
I remember sitting either on an examining table or a bed.
My head was swollen. This time my forehead, before the aspirate on the fluid, my forehead
was actually drooping down over my eyebrows. There was that much fluid in there, it was
that big, it was just drooping down in front.
And this was, do you think this was when you were a walker?
Yeah.
So, just, so the swelling was almost immediate, huh?
Yeah, it was a lot of loose fluid. See, the damaged blood vessels were leaking fluid into the, into the scalp. Lots of it.
And over time, let's see if this shows it. Now, this is on Monday.
see? That's loose blood, see, that's coming down out of here, all around my nose and everything
there. My entire face turned yellow all the way down to where the interstitial tissues
are attached to the collarbone and the sternum. So I was yellow like a Chinese or an Oriental.
all over my face and down to that V, and from there on I was white.
But as far as that free blood could drain, I turned yellow and black, just like a bruise.
And that's the beginning of it there, but that progressed and got worse and worse as time went by.
While you were at the hospital, he said that Captain Kittinger was trying to contact Dr.
Staff, John Paul Staff, at Holloman.
No, not at Holloman.
He was at Wright Patterson.
He was at Wright Patterson.
Yeah.
By this time, was he an Aeromed laboratory commander?
Yes, yes.
He was an Aeromed commander.
Okay.
So Kittinger was reporting in to him?
And I'm not sure that we were as much concerned about reporting into him as we were establishing
our identity.
For?
For the security people.
For the security people.
Yeah.
Did they?
That was my impression of what the urgency of getting ahold of staff was.
There would be two things.
One, staff hearing that there had been a problem and him not knowing about it, so we wanted
to report to him.
yeah, we had an accident, but everybody's all right. And no great damage done, no damage to
the gondola or anything like that. We just got cut up a little bit, but everything's fine.
And the other was, I think the more urgent part of it was the identity problem.
Well, the day SAC was damn serious about security.
Did you have...
So was this commonplace in the Air Force,
as far as getting involved with SAC?
Oh, yes, absolutely, absolutely.
Security of the Nuclear Strike Force was paramount.
SAC ran the Air Force in those days.
I see. But you weren't sacked. Did you ever have to go run in with these guys?
Run ins with them? Security people in sack bases? Yeah, lots of times. And single engine
airplanes around, you're always going to wind up in a position where, I don't care if it
is a sack base, I've got to land. I've got to get fuel or something, or the weather's
bad and you can't go any further and you've got to land. It was always, if you landed
going to get interrogated by the security people.
Curtis LeMay liked better than to send out people that just suddenly showed up and landed on the base.
Everybody said, well, it's an Air Force airplane, so it's okay.
And then out would come his IG and just really rip everybody,
probably more wing commanders lost their jobs over that kind of thing than anything else that happened.
So, Captain Joe Kittinger, how would you describe him physically?
Joe was about average height. He was always a little bit on the heavy side, not necessarily
not fat, but he was stocky built, red hair, freckle face.
What kind of red hair? Was it a little red or?
It was red. It was carrot red.
He was a pretty formidable figure, you think about that.
Well, we didn't think so. We were just all captains together.
Did you, I know you were getting treated, but at that time did you hear or discussion or overhear any altercations that Colonel Kittinger may have gotten into that day?
No, never heard anything. Never heard anything.
They were mostly involved in the physical exam and stuff like that.
Joe and Bill were off doing whatever they were doing.
Would you, with Colonel, Captain Kittinger at that time,
would he have ever had an NCO that assisted him on this particular morning
who would have been a black man that you can remember?
I don't remember that.
I really don't remember a black NCO.
I know that there were a lot of people ever involved in helping in the operation.
early but I can't remember him specifically. So my contacts with that crew, the actual flight crew
and everything was at night because that's when we went down and flayed the balloon and made the
takeoff was after dark. Didn't belong to my operation back at Wright-Patt and all the two
flights that we made were the only two times I was ever at Holloman so I didn't know any of those
people at all. And Joe flew out of there all the time, so he knew them quite well.
Okay. Getting back to Holloman when you're getting ready to leave, did...
Were you... Who else was on the 131? Was it a regularly scheduled flight, or...?
They took us back to Wright-Patt. I don't recall. They had, in those days, kind of a shuttle service that went around out of
AFSC headquarters at, not headquarters, but out of Wright-Patterson.
And this could have been one of the shuttles or they sent some airplane out special or I just don't know.
If they returned us on Monday and opened this accident,
I don't know whether to send somebody out special if it was one of the shuttles that was just moving around at the time.
And it could have been anybody, I could have known.
When we got back to Wright-Patt, of course that R&D community there, even though it was a huge base and everything,
It was a pretty small knit community anyway, but I had talked to my wife just from the
minute I got back to Holloman just to let her know that I had been in an accident, but
I wasn't heard because I didn't know what kind of publicity had gotten out in the newspapers
or anything.
And I told her I was just fine, a little banged up, but nothing to be worried about.
But I looked awful.
And when I got off the airplane at Wright-Patt, and of course the base operations, they called
her and told her what time I was going to be there on the airplane.
So she was there to meet me.
And when I came down the stairs of the airplane, and she was there on the ramp close to the
steps, and she saw me and realized that was me, she just burst into tears because I looked
I looked like I ought to be more dead than alive.
And that was sort of the reaction I got from everybody.
In fact, when I went back to the lab the next day on the job,
I walked in and stood at the desk in front of my secretary.
My secretary was talking to her and mentioned this or that,
and all of a sudden there was this long pause and she looked at me and she said,
Captain Fulcher, is that you? And she burst into tears because she had been talking to me
not realizing who I was. That's how different I really looked.
And with my eyes swollen shut and black marks all over my face from that blood
I just looked like somebody that evoked immediate compassionate sympathy.
